did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a series of verbs describing widespread destruction: the Lord empties the earth, lays it waste, twists its surface, and scatters its inhabitants.
The destruction erases social distinctions: the people, priest, servant, master, maidservant, mistress, buyer, seller, lender, and borrower are all mentioned alike.
The reason for the destruction is expressed in moral and covenantal terms: the inhabitants of the earth have violated the teaching, broken the law, and breached the everlasting covenant.
The earth is described as devouring a curse, while its inhabitants bear the guilt; as a result, very few people will remain.
Joy disappears along with wine and the vine: the new wine mourns, the vine languishes, and the joyful-hearted sigh.
The chapter emphasizes the end of music and public celebration by mentioning the tambourines, joyful noise, and lyre.
The remnant left after the destruction is compared to the gleanings remaining in a vineyard and to olives left after the harvest—very little of what was there before.

Songs of praise to the Lord are heard from the earth, but alongside this description of singing comes the prophet’s cry over the treachery of the treacherous; thus the chapter creates tension between hope and sin.
The phrase “terror and pit and snare” presents a sequence of dangers: whoever flees from the terror may fall into the pit, and whoever climbs out of the pit may be caught in the snare.
At the end of the chapter, the sun and moon lose their brightness compared with the Lord’s reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, where his glory is revealed before the elders.
